prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength are interrogated without light shift, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have moved from magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) to optical lattice clocks (B041) as my preferred single-part prize. My round-1 file already conceded that the clocks are unquestionably mature, and the exchange has sharpened what I meant by that. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a specific physical idea: a trapping potential that leaves the clock transition unperturbed, so that thousands of atoms are interrogated with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. It has been realised and compared at the 10^-18 level by independent laboratories in Japan, the USA, Germany, France and elsewhere, with agreeing numbers. That is the standard of independent confirmation I ask of any claim. The many-body coherence and spin-correlation physics in these clocks, and the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift they resolve, are condensed-matter-like quantum behaviour that I as a theorist of interacting systems take seriously, and I think that answers part of my own earlier worry that this is merely better measurement. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist. The citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice so that it is clearly separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: My reservation, which I now regard as a point of emphasis and not a reason to oppose, is that part of the fundamental-physics payoff (varying constants, dark matter limits, a redefined second) is still prospective, and the discovery content lies in instrumentation. The 2005 and 2012 prizes cover neighbouring ground, so the committee would be choosing a third metrology prize in twenty years. Credit is also incomplete: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made essential contributions to the concept and to accuracy evaluation, and I cannot verify priority at that level of detail, since atomic physics is outside my competence. As for B017, I still hold that the correlated phases are real and reproduced, but I cannot overcome the objection of six colleagues that the interpretation is moving. I accept that a prize now would rest partly on an open question.

responses.point: Mehlig would be more comfortable with B017 if the citation were restricted to flat bands and correlated insulators, and says the mechanism of the superconductivity is a sentence the committee cannot yet state.
responses.response: I take that restriction seriously and it is a fair drafting solution: flat bands and correlated insulators are the best-reproduced and best-matched to the continuum theory. But it would drop the superconductivity, which is what made the 2018 result a discovery, and I do not think a truncated citation fixes the real problem, which is that the field is still moving. I therefore concede the timing point to you and the others. On B027, I still see the overlap with the 2016 prize as real, and Mehlig's own note that hard disks melt first order weakens the universality claim for an award, so I will not support it as a first choice, although I would value your reading of the colloid experiments.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B004 and calls it more settled than twisted graphene, with fifteen years of confirmation, while conceding that the 2016 prize is close.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and quality, and I keep B004 as an alternative. Z2 topological insulators do not need a magnetic field and so are not strictly the quantum Hall physics of 2016, but they are the same conceptual family of topological band classification, and the attribution problem remains. The Molenkamp experiment rests on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Hasan and Fu, Kane and Mele carry the 3D case. A three-person set that is fair to all of them does not exist, and the committee must not choose a prize that has to omit a principal. You asked about the lattice clock as a discovery. My answer is that I now accept it as discovery-grade physics, because it opens regimes of many-body quantum coherence and resolves redshifts that could not be accessed before, so I would not call your reservation about novelty a disqualifier, and I hope you can accept the same.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the clocks are a measurement advance that changes what physics can observe, with confirmation across independent laboratories and a clean pair of names, and notes that support comes from members of different specialties.
responses.response: That argument persuades me, in particular the point that the support spans different specialties and is not confined to atomic physicists. As a theorist I attach weight to the fact that the claim is repeatedly and independently tested by comparison between clocks, which is a stricter test than most of condensed matter physics can offer. I also agree with Kroll that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly. I have used that wording in my citation. I would add a caution to Kroll's cautions about priority: the committee should check Takamoto's and Derevianko's roles before the final text, but I do not think they change the pair of names.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether the condensed-matter members regard the core discovery of B017 as stable enough, independent of the pairing mechanism, and says he would not rule it out in a few years.
responses.response: I will answer as a condensed-matter member. The existence of the correlated insulating and superconducting phases at the magic angle is stable. It has been reproduced many times, and the fractional Chern insulators in moire systems are a sign of lasting impact. But I did compare it with high-Tc superconductors, and I now think that comparison cuts the other way. Those were rewarded after about a year, with the mechanism still open, but the committee then was rewarding a surprise, whereas this committee is asked to judge a discovery whose interpretation Danielsson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson all find unsettled. I will not insist, and I agree it is better to return to it in a few years.

responses.point: Johansson notes that the lattice clock's headline justification shifts between metrology and fundamental physics, that constant-variation results are so far null, and that the citation should not claim more than the concept and first record-level realisations.
responses.response: I agree with the drafting caution, and my citation therefore leads with the clock itself and the 10^-18 level and says nothing about new physics found. Null results on varying constants are still results that bound physics, but the prize should reward what is shown, an invention and its record realisation. On B028, my position is unchanged. I still think the closeness to the 2025 prize, which I chaired, and the Blais-Girvin omission are problems, and I appreciate that you have moved it to an alternative and disclosed your proximity. I would ask that the committee discount the B028 opening ranks from members with the closest ties, as the chair's summary suggests.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can word the citation so that it rests on magic-wavelength lattice trapping and the 10^-18 realisation, and separates the prize from the 2005 and 2012 awards without implying that NIST, PTB and SYRTE contributed nothing.
I cannot check priority among Katori, Takamoto, Lemonde, Derevianko and others, which lies in atomic physics, and I rely on colleagues for it.

Whether I am now deferring too much to the weight of first-place support, since I changed my position after most colleagues objected to B017's maturity. I believe the scientific reasons are sufficient, but I cannot exclude that the number of supporters influenced me.
Whether a prize in precision measurement for the third time in twenty years is consistent with the committee's wish to reward new quantum behaviour in matter.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and no tie to any other credited candidate on the shortlist. My ties are to Uppsala, Los Alamos co-authors and committee colleagues, and none of them are credited. I note that I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize, which bears on my view of the timing of B028, and that I have moved away from my own field's candidate, B017, as my preferred choice.
